analysis.one_liner: Bans piece-rate garment pay, makes brands liable for wage theft, and subsidizes bringing garment jobs to America.
analysis.headline: The FABRIC Act was introduced with 7 Democratic cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar garment employers from paying by the piece and instead require at least the federal hourly minimum wage, with bonuses still allowed. It would make fashion brands legally liable when their contractors cheat workers out of wages, and it would force garment manufacturers and contractors to register annually with the Labor Department, with fines up to $50 million for violations. It would also create a small federal office for the garment industry, award grants up to $5 million to domestic garment makers, and give a 30% tax credit to companies that move garment production from overseas into HUBZones and low-income communities in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers — in the United States an overwhelmingly immigrant, largely female workforce concentrated in places like Los Angeles and New York — would gain an enforceable hourly minimum wage instead of piece rates that can leave them below minimum wage. The bill's joint-liability provision targets the brands at the top of the supply chain, giving workers a solvent party to sue when a contractor shuts down owing back pay. Compliant domestic manufacturers and nonprofits would also gain, through a $40 million grant program (awards up to $5 million) and a 30% tax credit for relocating garment production from abroad to economically distressed U.S. areas.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits paying garment workers by the piece and requires at least the federal hourly minimum wage, while still allowing incentive bonuses — addressing a pay structure long associated with sub-minimum earnings in sweatshops.

Makes brands that contract for garment manufacturing ('brand guarantors') jointly liable with their contractors for wage-law violations, so workers chasing unpaid wages can pursue the brand rather than only a shell contractor, and adds doubled liquidated damages.

Requires annual registration of garment manufacturers and contractors with the Department of Labor — including proof of workers' compensation coverage and disclosure of prior wage-law violations — and lets the Secretary suspend or revoke certificates or impose civil penalties up to $50 million.

Creates a Garment Industry office inside the Labor Department (authorized at $10 million plus $3 million a year) and a $40 million grant program, capped at $5 million per award, that prioritizes unionized shops and minority-, women-, and veteran-owned manufacturers.
Adds a tax credit worth 30% of the cost of moving a garment business unit from overseas into a HUBZone or low-income U.S. community, allowed only if the company's total domestic employment rises.

Exempts unionized workers only where a collective bargaining agreement provides overtime above 1.5x, a minimum wage at least 10% above the higher of the state or federal minimum, and a wage-dispute process — a carve-out that preserves negotiated deals only when they beat the bill's floor.

analysis.who_pays: Fashion brands and their subcontracted garment contractors would bear the main costs: brand guarantors face joint liability (doubled liquidated damages) for supplier wage violations, and shops would pay a $200 annual registration fee, document their ownership and compliance history, and absorb the cost of moving from piece rates to hourly wages. Taxpayers would fund the authorized $50 million in program spending and forgo revenue from the new insourcing tax credit. Consumers could see marginally higher apparel prices where piece-rate savings disappear.

drawbacks.text: The registration regime demands unusually sensitive data — Social Security numbers of owners, officers, and the 10 largest shareholders, plus the names and addresses of every production employee — and the $50 million maximum civil penalty is far above typical labor-law penalties, raising proportionality and privacy concerns for small businesses.
Banning piece rate could cut earnings for the fastest, most productive sewers who out-earn an hourly floor, even though the bill allows incentive bonuses on top of hourly pay.

Joint liability plus registration costs could push marginal domestic contractors out of business or production offshore, hurting the very workers the bill aims to protect; the bill contains no assessment of that risk.
The 30% insourcing credit is an open-ended tax expenditure whose cost depends entirely on how much production companies choose to relocate, with no cap stated in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core worker protections respond to a real and well-documented problem: piece-rate pay and layered subcontracting are exactly the structures that let wage theft persist at the bottom of apparel supply chains, and joint liability is the one lever that reaches the brands with the money. The trade-offs are real but not fatal — the bonus allowance softens the piece-rate loss for fast workers, the union carve-out is drafted to require above-bill standards, and the registration/penalty provisions could be calibrated in rulemaking. The weakest parts are the privacy-heavy registration data collection and the uncapped insourcing tax credit, which spends public money to subsidize relocations companies might make anyway. On balance, a defensible bill whose main cost falls on brands and noncompliant shops rather than on workers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor and Ways and Means committees from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney (D-NY) introduced the FABRIC Act on July 21, 2022, with Representatives Ross, Dingell, Carson, Nadler, and Khanna as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to two committees — Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — a split referral that meant both would have to act before it could advance.
Seven Democratic cosponsors signed on in total, but no Republican did, and the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either committee.
The action record shows no movement after the initial referral, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill; all introduced bills die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fashion brands and garment contractors that rely on piece-rate pay and layered subcontracting are better off, because joint liability and registration never took effect; the domestic piece-rate status quo continued for the workers the bill would have covered.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's sponsor and all 7 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, while the Democratic-run committees that never scheduled it also belong to the same party.

industries.industry: Fashion brands and apparel retailers (brand guarantors)
industries.note: Joint liability would make brands financially responsible for wage violations anywhere in their contractor chain, ending the insulation that layered subcontracting provides. Their savings under the current system come directly from the wage practices the bill targets.

They would face piece-rate elimination, $200 annual registration, disclosure requirements, and penalties up to $50 million — but the same bill offers them $5 million grants and a 30% insourcing tax credit. Compliant shops gain a moat against competitors that survive on wage theft.

industries.industry: Domestic apparel manufacturing and its workforce
industries.note: The insourcing credit and grant program are designed to pull garment production back from overseas into HUBZones and low-income communities, with priority for unionized and minority- or women-owned shops.
